# ACT New Zealand

> Classical-liberal / right-libertarian party, founded in 1994. It has been a junior partner in the National-led coalition since November 2023.
> **Leader:** [David Seymour](./people/david-seymour/README.md) (since October 2014). He has been Deputy Prime Minister since 31 May 2025 and is also Minister for Regulation.
> **Deputy leader:** [Nicole McKee](./people/nicole-mckee/README.md) (since 28 June 2026, replacing Brooke van Velden, who is retiring at the election). **President:** John Windsor.

- 2026 policies: **[./policies/README.md](./policies/README.md)**
- Track record (promises vs delivery, reliability, alignment): **[./track-record.md](./track-record.md)**
- Promise data: [`data/promises/act.json`](../../data/promises/act.json)

## Quick facts

| | |
|---|---|
| Founded | 1993 as the Association of Consumers and Taxpayers (pressure group); party from 1994. Founders: Sir Roger Douglas and Derek Quigley |
| Ideology | Classical liberalism, right-libertarianism, conservatism (Wikipedia); describes itself as standing for "one law for all", smaller government and individual freedom |
| Seats (54th Parliament) | 11 of 123: Epsom (Seymour), Tāmaki (van Velden) and 9 list MPs |
| 2023 party vote | 8.64% (246,409 votes), its best result ever |
| 2026 polling | Roughly 6–11% across 2026 polls. In October 2026 polls: 9–11% |
| In government | Support partner for National 2008–2017. Coalition partner since 2023: 3 Cabinet ministers plus ministers outside Cabinet |

## History

**Origins (1993–2004).** ACT grew out of the "Backbone Club" of Labour MPs who backed Roger Douglas's free-market reforms ("Rogernomics"). It began as a pressure group and became a party to contest the first MMP election. Its platform was based on Douglas's book *Unfinished Business*. Under Richard Prebble (leader 1996–2004) it won 6.1% in 1996, 7.0% in 1999 and 7.1% in 2002.

**Collapse and the Epsom lifeline (2005–2011).** After Prebble left, ACT fell to 1.5% in 2005. It survived only because Rodney Hide won Epsom. In 2008 it took 3.65% and five MPs and gave National confidence and supply: Hide became Minister of Local Government and Regulatory Reform, and Heather Roy a minister outside Cabinet. Former National leader Don Brash joined ACT and took over in April 2011 when Hide stepped aside, amid internal pressure on Hide's leadership.

**The one-MP era (2011–2020).** From 2011 to 2020 ACT had a single MP, every time through Epsom, where National signalled that its voters should give ACT their electorate vote:

| Election | Leader | Party vote | Seats | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2011 | Don Brash (John Banks led after the election) | 1.07% | 1 (Banks, Epsom) | Confidence and supply with National. Banks became Minister for Regulatory Reform and Small Business. The deal brought in charter (partnership) schools |
| 2014 | Jamie Whyte (Seymour from 3 Oct 2014) | 0.69% | 1 (Seymour, Epsom) | Confidence and supply. Seymour became Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Education (charter schools) and Regulatory Reform |
| 2017 | David Seymour | 0.50% | 1 | Opposition |
| 2020 | David Seymour | 7.58% | 10 | Opposition |
| 2023 | David Seymour | 8.64% | 11 | Coalition with National and NZ First |

- The 2011 "teapot tape" meeting between John Key and Banks in Epsom made the Epsom arrangement a national controversy. In 2014 John Key again encouraged National voters in Epsom to back Seymour, and about 60% of National voters there split their vote.
- John Banks retired as leader in 2014 to fight electoral-fraud charges over his 2010 Auckland mayoral campaign return. He was convicted in 2014, but the Court of Appeal quashed the conviction in 2015 and the Crown did not seek a retrial ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Banks_(New_Zealand_politician))).
- Leader Jamie Whyte (2014) attracted controversy over remarks on incest laws and on Māori "legal privilege". He resigned after the election.
- ACT's main achievement as a one-MP party was Seymour's **End of Life Choice Act**. It passed in 2019, was approved at the 2020 referendum and came into force on 7 November 2021.

**Breakthrough (2020).** ACT's rise to 7.6% and 10 MPs had three causes, according to analysts cited by Wikipedia. Seymour was the only MP to vote against the 2019 semi-automatic firearms ban, which drew gun owners (and firearms advocate Nicole McKee) to ACT. He was also a sharp critic of the COVID-19 response. And National was in leadership turmoil, while some NZ First voters were unhappy with Labour.

**2023 and coalition.** ACT won 8.64% and 11 seats, its best result. Brooke van Velden won Tāmaki, ACT's first electorate outside Epsom. In 2022 Seymour had said a Treaty-principles referendum would be a condition of coalition. In the end ACT signed a coalition agreement with National on 24 November 2023 that did not include a referendum (see below).

## In government, 2023–2026

**Ministers:** Seymour (Regulation; Associate Finance, Health (Pharmac) and Education; Deputy PM from 31 May 2025), Brooke van Velden (Internal Affairs; Workplace Relations and Safety), Nicole McKee (Courts; Associate Justice (firearms)), Karen Chhour (Children; Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence), Andrew Hoggard (Biosecurity; Food Safety; Associate Agriculture). Simon Court was Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Infrastructure and RMA reform.

**Main coalition wins delivered** (details and sources in the [track record](./track-record.md)):
- **Ministry for Regulation**, established 1 March 2024 and funded by abolishing the Productivity Commission.
- **Regulatory Standards Act 2025**, passed 13 November 2025 (68–55), in force 1 January 2026.
- **Charter schools return**: legislation passed 25 September 2024; 18 schools open by July 2026, against Budget 2024 funding for 50.
- **Three-strikes law reinstated** (December 2024, introduced by McKee) and an **Arms Act rewrite** (Arms Act 2026, passed 29 July 2026).
- Interest deductibility for landlords restored (80% from April 2024, 100% from April 2025), pet bonds, 90-day trials for all employers, repeal of Fair Pay Agreements, and a Reserve Bank inflation-only mandate.
- Repeal of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act (April 2025), and a "need not race" directive for public services (September 2024).
- Deputy PM rotation: Seymour succeeded Winston Peters on 31 May 2025.

**What ACT did not get:**
- The **Treaty Principles Bill** was introduced and passed its first reading, as agreed. It drew a record 300,000 written submissions, about 90% opposed, and the Hīkoi mō te Tiriti. It was **voted down 112–11 at its second reading on 10 April 2025**, with National and NZ First voting against.
- No return of the public service to 2017 size, no abolition of "demographic" ministries, no repeal of the Zero Carbon Act, no reversal of the live-export ban, and no four-year-term referendum.
- ACT used the "agree to disagree" clause on the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill (July 2024), the scope of the firearms-registry review (May 2025) and the under-16 social media ban (August 2026). ACT also opposed the modern slavery bill (January 2026) and a gift-card expiry bill, and refused government backing for National's social-media bill in May 2025.

**Controversies (factual):**
- In June 2024 Stuff reported allegations of bullying and a "culture of fear" during ACT's 2023 campaign. The party said an independent review had been carried out and its recommendations accepted.
- The 2025 Equal Pay Amendment Act, led by Brooke van Velden as Workplace Relations Minister, passed under urgency. It raised the thresholds for pay-equity claims, and critics say it ended 33 active claims ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_Pay_Amendment_Act_2025)).
- The redesigned school lunch programme was criticised for meal quality.
- In June 2026 Porirua candidate Lyra Yan Zhang left the list after failing to declare past membership of the China Zhi Gong Party.

## Money: donations

- In 2022 ACT received over $2 million in large donations, including several rich-list donors giving $100,000 each ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2023/05/electoral-donations-for-2022-national-received-more-than-10-times-what-labour-got.html)).
- ACT declared about $4.3m in donations in its 2023 return, behind National's $10.4m and Labour's $4.8m ([Weekend Herald](https://www.pressreader.com/new-zealand/weekend-herald/20240504/281578065741385)).
- In the 2025 annual returns ACT overtook Labour in donations ([RNZ, 7 May 2026](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/594551/national-tops-party-donations-list-act-overtakes-labour)).
- Wikipedia's 2026 election tracker lists about $4.79m in declared donations as of late October 2026. Donors include Nick Mowbray ($225,000), Brian Cartmell ($200,000), Greymouth Petroleum subsidiary GMP Environmental ($100,000) and Van Den Brink Karaka ($100,000). ACT reported $2.35m raised in 2026 by 24 September ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_New_Zealand_general_election)).

## 2026 pitch

The campaign was launched at Shed 10, Auckland, on 28 June 2026 under the theme **"Lock Labour Out, Unlock New Zealand's Potential"**. Seymour named three focuses: government waste, cutting business restrictions, and equal rights under the law ([Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/29-06-2026/aura-edits-and-protests-field-notes-from-the-act-partys-big-flash-rally), [speech on Scoop](https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2606/S00205.htm)). Broadcaster Paul Henry is fourth on the list. Headline promises, all sourced in [`act.json`](../../data/promises/act.json) and [policies](./policies/README.md):

- **Fiscal plan (11 October 2026):** gradually raise the NZ Super age by three months a year; pause Super Fund contributions; return non-welfare spending to 2017 per-capita levels; $653m in disability-benefit savings through independent medical certification; abolish demographic ministries; cut foreign aid ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/10/11/act-sets-out-plan-to-raise-retirement-age-cut-debt-and-spending/)).
- Freeze the adult minimum wage for three years and introduce a training wage; no tax on KiwiSaver earnings; repeal the Zero Carbon Act and net-zero target; abolish the Climate Change Commission.
- Disestablish the Waitangi Tribunal once historical claims are settled; entrench "equal rights" in constitutional statutes; end "race-based hiring" in the public service.
- Tougher immigration: deport serious non-citizen offenders, a five-year benefit stand-down for new residents, a $6-a-day surcharge on temporary work visas, and abolition of the permanent-resident visa category.
- Add burglary to three strikes; a $2b National Cancer Centre (Henry); raise Pharmac's share of the health budget; let pharmacists treat more conditions; supermarket competition through a one-stop consenting body, while opposing a forced break-up.

## Coalition stance for 2026

- ACT is campaigning to re-form the National-led government and keep Labour out ("Lock Labour Out").
- Seymour defended voters' right to split their vote, after National's John Key and Christopher Luxon urged National supporters not to.
- ACT and NZ First have clashed publicly. After NZ First pledged to repeal the Regulatory Standards Act it had voted for, Seymour accused Peters of bad faith and of positioning for a deal with Labour ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulatory_Standards_Act_2025)).

## Leaders

Roger Douglas (1994–96) · Richard Prebble (1996–2004) · Rodney Hide (2004–11) · Don Brash (2011) · John Banks (2012–14) · Jamie Whyte (2014) · David Seymour (2014–). Deputy leaders since 2017: Beth Houlbrooke (2017–20), Brooke van Velden (2020–26), Nicole McKee (2026–).

# New Zealand Labour Party (Rōpū Reipa o Aotearoa)

> Centre-left, social-democratic party; New Zealand's oldest current political party (founded 1916).
> **Leader:** [Chris Hipkins](./people/chris-hipkins/) (since 22 Jan 2023) · **Deputy:** [Carmel Sepuloni](./people/carmel-sepuloni/) (since 7 Nov 2023) ·
> **Finance spokesperson:** [Barbara Edmonds](./people/barbara-edmonds/) · **2026 slogan:** "Better Starts Now" ·
> **Status (Oct 2026):** Official Opposition, 34 MPs · **Last in government:** 2017–2023
>
> See also: [Track record & promise tracker](./track-record.md) · [2026 policies](./policies/README.md) · [Promise data (JSON)](../../data/promises/labour.json)

*Compiled 23 October 2026. Every factual claim is linked to a source; where sources disagree or we could not verify something, that is said explicitly.*

---

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Founded | 7 July 1916, by trade unions and socialist groups ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)) |
| Ideology | Social democracy; constitution still states democratic-socialist principles; in practice pragmatic centre-left ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)) |
| Times in government | 6 (1935–49, 1957–60, 1972–75, 1984–90, 1999–2008, 2017–23) ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)) |
| Current MPs | 34 (17 electorate, 17 list) ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)) |
| 2023 result | 26.91% party vote, 34 seats — down from 50.01% / 65 seats in 2020 |
| 2026 polling | ~27–31% in October 2026 polls, down from ~34–37% in the first half of 2026 (see below) |
| Donations | $3.27m declared electoral donations 2025–Oct 2026 (third behind National and ACT) |
| Party colour | Red |

---

## History

**Origins (1916–1935).** Labour was formed in 1916 as the political wing of the union movement. Its early leaders (Harry Holland, Peter Fraser, Bob Semple, Paddy Webb) opposed WWI conscription and some were jailed. It won 8 seats in 1919 and became the official Opposition in 1926; radical policies such as the "usehold" (state leasehold) land policy were dropped during the 1920s ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

**First Labour Government (1935–1949)** under Michael Joseph Savage and Peter Fraser built the modern welfare state (state housing, social security, free health care). **Second (1957–60)** under Walter Nash and **Third (1972–75)** under Norman Kirk/Bill Rowling were single-term governments.

**Fourth Labour Government (1984–1990)** under David Lange and Finance Minister Roger Douglas carried out sweeping market liberalisation ("Rogernomics") — deregulation, corporatisation and privatisation — which split the party and its union base, and also made New Zealand nuclear-free. Membership collapsed in the 1980s–90s ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

**Fifth Labour Government (1999–2008)** under Helen Clark (three election wins) governed in MMP coalitions/support arrangements (Alliance, Progressives, United Future, NZ First, Greens). It introduced KiwiSaver, Working for Families, the NZ Super Fund, Kiwibank, interest-free student loans and NCEA; the 2004 foreshore and seabed controversy led to the breakaway Māori Party ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

**Opposition (2008–2017)** — four leaders in nine years (Goff, Shearer, Cunliffe, Little). The 2014 result (25.13%) was Labour's worst since 1922. Policies run in 2011 and 2014 — a capital gains tax, raising the pension age to 67, NZ Power, KiwiAssure — were all dropped by Andrew Little after 2014 (see [track record](./track-record.md#1-opposition-era-promises-2011--2014)). With Labour polling at 24%, Little stood down on 1 August 2017 and Jacinda Ardern took over seven weeks before the election ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

**Sixth Labour Government (2017–2023)** — see [Government periods](#government-periods-2008-2026) below.

**Opposition again (2023–2026).** Hipkins was re-elected leader after the 2023 defeat; veterans Grant Robertson, Kelvin Davis and Rino Tirikatene (2024) and David Parker (2025) left Parliament. Labour called for recognition of Palestinian statehood (April 2024) and Hipkins said a Labour government would not be part of AUKUS (December 2024). Several Labour members' bills passed with cross-party support (e.g. Camilla Belich's wage-theft and pay-secrecy bills, Deborah Russell's divorce-wait exemption for family-violence victims) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party); [54th Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament)).

## Ideology and principles

Labour's 1916 objective was "the socialisation of the means of production, distribution and exchange"; the socialist objective was dropped in 1951. The current constitution lists democratic-socialist principles — management of natural resources for all, equal access regardless of wealth, co-operation in economic relations "to ensure a just distribution of wealth", the right to work, people "more important than property", **honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi**, international co-operation, and equality regardless of race, sex, sexuality, gender identity, age, religion or disability. Observers describe its policy as pragmatic social democracy with social-liberal positions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

Core voter base today: young people, urban workers, public servants, and Māori and Pasifika communities ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

## Organisation and union links

- **Structure:** electorate branches and special branches (Māori, Pasifika, women, rainbow, university, etc.) → Labour Electorate Committees → six regional conferences → **Annual Conference** (called Congress in election years), the supreme body. The **New Zealand Council** is the governing executive; a **Policy Council** elected each term writes the platform and manifesto ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).
- **Caucus elects Cabinet:** unusually, Labour's caucus — not the leader — elects its ministers ([Wikipedia: Leader of the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).
- **Leadership rules (2021):** a candidate needs two-thirds of caucus; failing that, an electoral college of caucus 40% / members 40% / **affiliated unions 20%** decides ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).
- **Affiliated unions:** 11 affiliated unions in 2023, paying a levy by membership; the CTU president speaks at the annual conference ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)). Union influence over leadership votes is a recurring criticism. Policy closely aligned with unions in government: Fair Pay Agreements, doubled sick leave, pay equity settlements, repeal of 90-day trials for larger firms.
- **Young Labour** is the youth wing. The party's handling of 2018 Young Labour camp assaults and of 2019 complaints against a staffer drew heavy criticism; party president Nigel Haworth resigned in 2019 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Labour_Government_of_New_Zealand)).
- **Party presidents** (recent): Andrew Little (2009–11), Moira Coatsworth (2011–15), Nigel Haworth (2015–19), Claire Szabó (2019–22), Jill Day (2022–). *Dates from Wikipedia's list of presidents; not independently re-verified.*

## Election results 2008–2023

| Election | Leader | Party vote | Seats | Electorate / list | Change | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2008 | Helen Clark | 33.99% | 43 | 21 / 22 | −7 | Lost office to National |
| 2011 | Phil Goff | 27.48% | 34 | 22 / 12 | −9 | Opposition |
| 2014 | David Cunliffe | 25.13% | 32 | 27 / 5 | −2 | Opposition (worst since 1922) |
| 2017 | Jacinda Ardern | 36.89% | 46 | 29 / 17 | +14 | **Government** (coalition with NZ First; Green confidence & supply) |
| 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | 50.01% | 65 | 46 / 19 | +19 | **Majority government** — first single-party majority under MMP |

Sources: Wikipedia articles on the [2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_New_Zealand_general_election), [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_New_Zealand_general_election), [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_New_Zealand_general_election), [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election), [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_New_Zealand_general_election) and [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_New_Zealand_general_election) elections (copies in `raw/elections/`); official figures at [electionresults.govt.nz](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/).

**Trend.** Labour's vote has swung more violently than any other party's under MMP: from 25% (2014) to 50% (2020) and back to 27% (2023). The 2020 landslide drew in former National voters in a COVID "rally" election; in 2023 Labour faced a ~23-point swing, losing Auckland heartland seats, five Māori seats to Te Pāti Māori and two Wellington seats to the Greens ([Wikipedia 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_New_Zealand_general_election)). Detailed analysis: [track record — trends](./track-record.md#8-trends).

## Government periods 2008–2026

| Period | Arrangement | Leader / PM |
|---|---|---|
| 2008–2017 | Opposition to the Fifth National Government (Key, English) | Goff → Shearer → Cunliffe → Little → Ardern |
| **Oct 2017 – Oct 2020** | **Coalition with NZ First** (Winston Peters Deputy PM) + **confidence & supply from the Greens** (Green ministers outside Cabinet). NZ First vetoed or diluted several Labour policies (CGT, three-strikes repeal, light rail, water charges, 90-day trials, Fair Pay Agreements). | Jacinda Ardern |
| **Nov 2020 – Nov 2023** | **Labour majority (65/120)**; non-binding **cooperation agreement with the Greens** (James Shaw and Marama Davidson ministers outside Cabinet). No partner could block policy. | Ardern → Hipkins (Jan 2023) |
| Nov 2023 – | Official Opposition to the National–ACT–NZ First coalition | Hipkins |

Sources: [Wikipedia: Sixth Labour Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Labour_Government_of_New_Zealand); [Wikipedia: Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party).

Key events of the Sixth Labour Government: Christchurch mosque attacks and semi-automatic firearms ban (2019); Whakaari eruption (2019); COVID-19 elimination strategy, wage subsidy and border closure (2020–21); abandonment of elimination after Delta and the 2022 Parliament occupation; 7.3% inflation (June 2022, a 32-year high) ([1News](https://1news.co.nz/2022/07/18/inflation-rises-to-73-a-32-year-high/)); Ardern's resignation and Hipkins' "policy bonfire" (2023); Auckland floods and Cyclone Gabrielle (2023). Ministerial resignations or sackings included Clare Curran, Meka Whaitiri, Phil Twyford, David Clark, Stuart Nash, Kiri Allan, and [Michael Wood](./people/michael-wood/) (2023) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

## Current caucus (54th Parliament)

Labour holds **34 seats** (17 electorates, 17 list) ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)). Changes during the term: Andrew Little (replaced by [Camilla Belich](./people/camilla-belich/), Dec 2023), Rino Tirikatene ([Tracey McLellan](./people/tracey-mclellan/)), Kelvin Davis ([Shanan Halbert](./people/shanan-halbert/)), Grant Robertson ([Glen Bennett](./people/glen-bennett/)) in 2024, and David Parker ([Vanushi Walters](./people/vanushi-walters/), May 2025) ([Wikipedia: 54th Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament)).

Senior figures and 2026 list ranks (list per [policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)): 1 [Chris Hipkins](./people/chris-hipkins/) (Remutaka) · 2 [Carmel Sepuloni](./people/carmel-sepuloni/) · 3 [Barbara Edmonds](./people/barbara-edmonds/) (finance) · 4 [Willie Jackson](./people/willie-jackson/) (justice) · 5 [Megan Woods](./people/megan-woods/) · 6 [Ayesha Verrall](./people/ayesha-verrall/) (health) · 7 [Willow-Jean Prime](./people/willow-jean-prime/) · 8 [Vanushi Walters](./people/vanushi-walters/) (foreign affairs) · 9 [Cushla Tangaere-Manuel](./people/cushla-tangaere-manuel/) · 10 [Kieran McAnulty](./people/kieran-mcanulty/) (housing) · 11 [Rachel Brooking](./people/rachel-brooking/) · 12 [Ginny Andersen](./people/ginny-andersen/) (police/education). Former ministers [Phil Twyford](./people/phil-twyford/) (40), [Jan Tinetti](./people/jan-tinetti/) (15) and [Damien O'Connor](./people/damien-oconnor/) (16) are standing; [Michael Wood](./people/michael-wood/) is standing in Mt Roskill as an electorate-only candidate. Full roster: [people/](./people/).

Retiring at the 2026 election: Duncan Webb (Christchurch Central) and Greg O'Connor (did not seek a list place after his Ōhāriu seat was abolished) ([Wikipedia: 2026 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_New_Zealand_general_election); [The Post](https://www.thepost.co.nz/politics/361018627/greg-oconnor-not-standing-after-labour-list-process-makes-choosing-pope-look-transparent)).

On **23 October 2026** Labour's Tāmaki Makaurau candidate **Kerrin Leoni** resigned as a Labour candidate after footage showed her campaigning at a Mongrel Mob event; her name stays on the ballot without Labour's endorsement ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/election-2026-live-updates-kerrin-leoni-resigns-as-labour-candidate-after-campaigning-with-mongrel-mob/R5IJCEB4TNF3LETYQ5JOSBPH7A/); [Te Ao Māori News](https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2026/10/22/video-shows-labour-candidate-kerrin-leoni-at-mongrel-mob-event/)).

## 2026 polling

Labour led National in most polls from late 2025 to mid-2026 (often 34–37%), then slid through the campaign. October 2026 polls:

| 1News–Verian | 15–19 Oct | 27 | 32 |
| The Post/Freshwater | 9–19 Oct | 28.7 | 27.6 |
| 1News–Verian | 8–12 Oct | 28 | 28 |
| Anacta | 6–10 Oct | 29 | 28 |
| Taxpayers' Union–Curia | 1–5 Oct | 28.2 | 28.5 |
| 1News–Verian | 1–5 Oct | 28 | 29 |
| RNZ–Reid Research | 24 Sep–1 Oct | 30.8 | 25.9 |

For comparison, 1News–Verian had Labour on 37% in April 2026 and 32% in June. policy.nz gives a 2026 polling average of 31.3%. Sources: [Wikipedia: Opinion polling for the 2026 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opinion_polling_for_the_2026_New_Zealand_general_election) (copy in `raw/elections/`), [1News 20 Oct 2026](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/10/20/poll-national-jumps-leaving-labours-position-perilous/), [policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party). Cross-party series: [data/polls-2026.json](../../data/polls-2026.json).

## Donations and funding

- **$3,273,137.93** in declared electoral donations from 1 January 2025 to late October 2026 — behind National ($8.47m) and ACT ($4.79m). It includes $125,000 from the Mills Family Trust and $219,178 from the estate of Murray George Jones. In 2026 itself (to 24 September) Labour declared $869,896 from 15 donors ([Wikipedia: 2026 election — Fundraising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_New_Zealand_general_election), citing [RNZ's donations tracker](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/647946/political-donations-tracker-act-gets-another-dollar225-000-and-overall-parties-total-exceeds-2023-campaign)).
- policy.nz lists Labour's **2025** donations as $2,403,241.93 ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)).
- Affiliated unions pay levies to the party (see above).
- In 2020 the Serious Fraud Office investigated donations to Labour from two Chinese businessmen around the 2017 election; the party said it co-operated ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

## 2026 pitch and headline promises

Slogan **"Better Starts Now"**, launched 24 August 2026 ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/08/24/labour-reveals-its-2026-election-campaign-slogan/)). Labour is campaigning on cost of living, health access, jobs and "changing the government"; National has focused its attack on the capital gains tax. Headline commitments (full list and verbatim documents in [policies/](./policies/README.md)):

- **Capital gains tax** of 28% on residential and commercial property, excluding the family home and farms, from July 2027 — funding **up to three free GP visits a year** (Medicard), free maternity scans and free cervical screening ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/577021/labour-to-campaign-on-narrow-capital-gains-tax-no-wealth-tax)).
- **NZ Future Fund** to invest in infrastructure and NZ firms (details withheld until after the election) ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/10/20/nz-future-fund-labour-reveals-first-major-policy-for-next-election/); [NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/labour-admits-it-will-not-release-cornerstone-policy-costing-and-job-modelling-until-after-the-election-blames-treaty-of-waitangi-concerns/QNGXJK4SHZFOJB52WFCVHPLR4E/)).
- **$20/week public transport fare cap** in the three main cities ($10 elsewhere) ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360990643/labour-reveals-public-transport-fare-cap-long-awaited-election-policy)).
- **Fiscal strategy:** surplus by 2029/30, net debt ~20% of GDP, an independent budget office ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1081146/labour-releases-fiscal-strategy-promises-to-slash-debt)).
- **$4b for 6,000+ social housing places, school and hospital repairs** ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1552827/labour-pledges-4-billion-for-state-houses-school-repairs-and-hospitals)); **10% student-loan write-off** ($583.4m) ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/labour-kicks-off-campaign-after-national-hammers-home-tax-attack/JJ6SXVR3HJH2RB7BF4567UTSDI/)); **restore pay equity** and a $2.5b pay rise for care and support workers ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1718141/labour-releases-its-fiscal-plan-promises-pay-rise-for-care-and-support-workers)).
- **Cost of living / competition:** split supermarket wholesale from retail, ban price gouging, a "fair go" law on hidden fees, airline and bank competition measures ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1478631/labour-proposes-splitting-foodstuffs-and-woolworths-from-their-wholesale-arms)).
- **KiwiSaver:** compulsory employer contributions, 6% minimum ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1356180/labour-to-make-employer-contributions-to-kiwisaver-compulsory-if-elected)).
- **Reversals of coalition policy:** repeal the Regulatory Standards Act within 100 days; scrap youth boot camps; pause the NCEA/curriculum overhaul; restore school boards' Treaty obligations; restore locally made school lunches and rural school bus routes.
- **Rule-outs:** no GST rise in 2027, oppose fuel excise rises, no change to landlord interest deductibility.
- **Foreign policy:** recognise Palestine, sanctions on Israel, stay out of AUKUS, aid towards 0.7% of GDP ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/1528401/labour-sums-up-its-foreign-policy-approach-as-independent-principled-and-unafraid)).

How these compare with Labour's past delivery: [track record §9](./track-record.md#9-what-the-record-suggests-for-2026-promises).

## Coalition stances for 2026

# United Future New Zealand (UnitedFuture)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status (Oct 2026)** | **Dissolved** — disbanded November 2017; registration cancelled 28 February 2018 |
| **Founded** | 2000 (merger of United New Zealand and Future New Zealand); contested elections 2002–2017 |
| **Leaders** | Peter Dunne (2000–2017); Damian Light (Aug–Nov 2017) |
| **Ideology** | Centrist; originally liberal-conservative / Christian-democratic, rebranded as "a modern centre party" in 2007 |
| **Best result** | 6.69% and 8 seats (2002) |
| **In government** | Confidence-and-supply partner of Labour (2005–08) and National (2008–17); Dunne a minister outside Cabinet throughout |
| **Track record** | [track-record.md](track-record.md) · [promise data](../../data/promises/united-future.json) |

## History

United Future was formed for the 2002 election by merging Peter Dunne's liberal United New Zealand (founded by
moderate Labour and National MPs in 1995) with Future New Zealand, a "secularised" successor to the Christian
Democrats. Helped by a strong televised-debate performance by Dunne, it won 6.7% and eight seats in 2002, but fell to
2.7% and three seats in 2005 and, after its socially conservative wing (Gordon Copeland, Larry Baldock and others)
left over the 2007 "anti-smacking" law to form what became the Kiwi Party, to a single seat — Dunne's — from 2008.
Dunne then rebranded the party as a moderate centrist party. [1]

After 2005 Dunne gave confidence and supply to Helen Clark's Labour-led government and became Minister of Revenue
outside Cabinet. From 2008 to 2017 he supported John Key's and Bill English's National-led governments under three
written agreements (2008, 2011, 2014) — see the [track record](track-record.md). [1][2]

### The 2011–2017 period covered by this archive

- **2011:** United Future won 0.60% of the party vote. Dunne held Ōhāriu by 1,392 votes over Labour's Charles
  Chauvel, who called National's soft-pedalling in the seat an "unprincipled political deal". [1][3][4]
- **2013 deregistration episode:** On 31 May 2013 the Electoral Commission cancelled the party's registration at its
  own request because it could not show 500 financial members. The Speaker ruled Dunne would sit as an independent
  and lose party-leader funding until it re-registered; the Commission re-registered the party on 13 August 2013. [1][5][6]
- **GCSB-report leak (June 2013):** Dunne resigned his ministerial portfolios on 7 June 2013 after declining to give
  the Henry inquiry all his emails with a Fairfax journalist about the leak of the Kitteridge report on the GCSB. In
  December 2013 Parliament's Privileges Committee found he had been entitled to refuse, and he was reinstated as a
  minister on 28 January 2014. [7][8]
- **2014:** 0.22% of the party vote; Dunne held Ōhāriu by 710 votes over Labour's Ginny Andersen. [3][9]
- **2017:** On 21 August 2017, citing polling and a "mood for change" in Ōhāriu, Dunne announced his retirement.
  Damian Light became leader on 23 August. The party won 0.07% (1,782 votes) and lost its only seat; Labour's Greg
  O'Connor won Ōhāriu. [1][10]
- **Dissolution:** The party's AGM voted to disband in November 2017; Light and Dunne confirmed it on 14 November and
  the registration was cancelled on 28 February 2018. [1][11]

## Ideology and policy

Its 2007 mission statement described "a modern centre party" promoting "strong families and vibrant communities" and
"a competitive economy ... through market policies where possible, and government where necessary". Signature
policies in this period were **income splitting/sharing** for families, **flexible ("flexi") superannuation**, health
and medicines policy (Medicines New Zealand, a bigger role for pharmacists), recreational hunting/fishing interests
(a Game Animal Council) and, in 2011, limits on state-asset sales. [1][2]

## Election results (2011–2017)

| Election | Party votes | Party vote % | Electorate seats | List seats | Total seats | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2011 | 13,443 | 0.60 | 1 (Ōhāriu) | 0 | **1** | Dunne majority 1,392 |
| 2014 | 5,286 | 0.22 | 1 (Ōhāriu) | 0 | **1** | Dunne majority 710 |
| 2017 | 1,782 | 0.07 | 0 | 0 | 0 | Dunne retired; Light led |

Earlier: 2002 6.69% (8 seats), 2005 2.67% (3 seats), 2008 0.87% (1 seat). Source for party votes: official results as
tabulated in the Wikipedia election articles. [3]

## MPs (2011–2017)

- **Peter Dunne** — MP for Ōhāriu (and its predecessors) 1984–2017; Minister of Revenue (2005–2013), Associate
  Minister of Health (2008–2013, 2014–2017), Associate Minister of Conservation (2011–2013, 2014–2017), Minister of
  Internal Affairs (2014–2017). No person folder exists for him in this archive. [7][12]

## Notable events and controversies

- Reliance on a single electorate seat, aided by National's low-key campaigns in Ōhāriu, drew criticism as a
  "deal" (2011). [4]
- 2013 membership/registration failure and loss of party funding. [5][6]
- 2013 resignation over the GCSB-report email inquiry, later vindicated by the Privileges Committee. [7]
- As Associate Health Minister Dunne steered the Psychoactive Substances Act 2013 (a regulated market for "legal
  highs") and later eased access to cannabis-based medicines. [7]

## Current status

Dissolved; it did not contest 2020, 2023 or 2026. Damian Light went into Auckland local politics and in 2022 was
elected to (and became chair of) the Howick Local Board. Peter Dunne has appeared as a political commentator since
retiring. [7][13]

# ACT New Zealand — 2026 election policies

Every 2026 general-election (7 November 2026) policy of ACT New Zealand that this archive could find: **110 policies** — 91 from [policy.nz](https://policy.nz/parties/act-party) and 19 additional policies found only on [act.org.nz](https://www.act.org.nz/policies) — backed by **128 full-text source documents** (54 policy page, 31 policy document (PDF), 27 press release, 14 policy index page, 1 press release (Scoop mirror), 1 fiscal plan microsite).

**How this was built** ([`tools/policies_act_fetch.py`](../../../tools/policies_act_fetch.py), [`tools/policies_act_build.py`](../../../tools/policies_act_build.py)):

- Starting point: the policy.nz dataset for ACT (`raw/policy.nz/parties/act-party.json`, 91 statements; policy.nz citations were accessed between 06 August 2026 and 19 October 2026). The **Why / How** text for those entries is policy.nz's neutral summary ("This party says …"), reproduced unchanged.
- Every cited source was fetched again directly from its origin (policy.nz cites Wayback Machine snapshots; the archived original URL was fetched instead) on 2026-10-23. HTML pages were reduced to their main content; PDFs were converted with `pdftotext` (designed multi-column PDFs can interleave sidebars with body text in reading order; the original PDFs are kept in `raw/party-docs/act/pdf/`).
- The full act.org.nz sitemap was crawled for policy pages (`/policies/*` index pages plus every policy landing page, excluding people, news archive and "ACT's Record" pages, which describe past actions rather than 2026 commitments). Every "Read the full policy" PDF linked from those pages was downloaded too.
- Policies on act.org.nz that policy.nz does not list were added with `summary_source: "archive"` (IDs `ACT-A01`…`ACT-A19`); their Why/How summaries were written for this archive from the linked ACT page and should be checked against the full text.
- Each policy links to the full verbatim text of its sources in [`documents/`](documents/). Duplicate PDFs (same file at several URLs) are stored once, with all URLs listed in the front matter.
- Structured data: [`policies.json`](policies.json).

> Summaries describe what ACT says it would do; they are not endorsements or fact-checks. ACT's own claims (costs, statistics) are reported as ACT's claims.

## Headline commitments

ACT's own [Fiscal Plan page](documents/fiscalplan.md) summarises its programme as (verbatim):

- Balance the books with no new taxes, putting much lower taxes within reach.
- Cut $9.5 billion a year from spending outside welfare and protected frontline services once fully implemented.
- Make government smaller and more accountable, with 19 departments and 18 ministers responsible for budgets and results.
- Remove tax on KiwiSaver investment earnings and discontinue the government contribution.
- Introduce a Carbon Tax Refund, returning net revenue from Emissions Trading Scheme auctions to New Zealanders.
- Gradually raise the NZ Super age to 67 by 2035, with compassionate early access for people who have spent much of their careers in physically demanding jobs.
- Fund better healthcare, expanding pharmacist care and setting aside around $2 billion as a funding contingency for a National Cancer Centre.

## Fiscal plan / alternative budget

ACT released its **[ACT Fiscal Plan 2026](documents/pdf-act-2026-fiscal-plan.md)** (12-page PDF, 11 October 2026; [original](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/pages/38747/attachments/original/1791599898/ACT_2026_Fiscal_Plan.pdf?1791599898)), with a landing page ([fiscalplan](documents/fiscalplan.md)) and an interactive debt microsite ([balancethebooks.nz](documents/fiscal-plan.md)). Key figures as stated in the PDF (all figures are ACT's; $ nominal):

- **Debt:** net core Crown debt (excluding NZ Super Fund) of $217 billion by June 2031, which ACT says is $12.4 billion lower than current Treasury forecasts (the PDF's "Headline Figures" page also describes it as "$12 billion lower than forecast in the Pre-election Fiscal Update"; the costing table shows 217.336 vs 229.769).
- **Operating balance:** OBEGAL surplus of $13.6 billion in 2030/31 (vs $8.9 billion under current Government plans); OBEGALx $16.4 billion (vs $11.7 billion); OBEGALx in small surplus in 2027/28, a year earlier than current plans; OBEGAL returns to a $5.1 billion surplus in 2028/29.
- **No new taxes; no broad-based tax cuts in this plan** — "several strategic tax cuts" instead: no tax on KiwiSaver earnings ($1.065bn in 2027/28 rising to $1.437bn in 2030/31), a Carbon Tax Refund (est. ~$100 per household), an uncapped donation tax credit, reformed crypto tax treatment, and $264m of targeted tax relief "to be announced".
- **New operating spending (outside the operating allowance), $445m in 2027/28 rising to $551m:** expanded pharmacy minor-ailments scheme, Local Tourism Dividend, Young Investors Fund (~$35m/yr, $500 for Year 11 students), Overstayers Investigation Unit ($60m/yr), rural crime funding, electronic money management for long-term Jobseeker recipients, Three Strikes for Burglary, Working with Children Check, independent school subsidy indexation, and a $100m/yr initiative "to be announced".
- **Savings:** future operating allowances cut from $2.4bn to $2bn a year (+$0.4bn in 2027/28 rising to +$1.6bn in 2030/31); non-welfare, non-frontline spending returned to 2017 levels per person (headline reductions $1.5bn in 2027/28, $2.8bn, $3.2bn, $2.4bn in 2030/31 — including abolishing demographic ministries ~$187m/yr and cutting foreign aid to 2017 levels excluding Ukraine ~$283m/yr); NZ Super age rising by three months a year to 67 by 2035 ($0.46bn rising to $1.89bn, less compassionate early access); five-year benefit stand-down for residence-class visa holders; tighter medical certification for health/disability benefits; replacing the KiwiSaver Government Contribution ($0.52–0.59bn/yr); lower financing costs ($452m by 2030/31).
- **Capital/non-operating:** $2m for anti-social noise cameras; $2bn contingency for a National Cancer Centre; $150m contingency for a new Epsom secondary school; maintain the suspension of NZ Super Fund contributions.
- The landing page states ACT would "Cut $9.5 billion a year from spending outside welfare and protected frontline services once fully implemented" and "Make government smaller and more accountable, with 19 departments and 18 ministers".
- The full costing table is reproduced (layout preserved) at the end of the [Fiscal Plan document](documents/pdf-act-2026-fiscal-plan.md).

### Make the abuse of a companion animal in a family violence situation a crime (POL54651)

***Key policy** (policy.nz) · Topics: community-and-inclusion, law-justice-and-government, animal-welfare, women, family-justice-and-safety, key-policies-community-and-inclusion · Summary: policy.nz*

**Statement:** Make the abuse of a companion animal in a family violence situation a crime

**Why:** This party says that pets are being threatened and abused to coerce people in family violence situations and prevent them from leaving. Research shows half of victims delay leaving a violent situation because they are concerned about their pets. Criminalising the abuse of animals in this context will give Police more tools to protect victims. States in Australia and the US have enacted similar laws and New Zealand needs to do the same.

**How:** This party would amend the Crimes Act to make abusing a pet with the goal of coercion an offence punishable by a maximum seven years in prison. Protection orders would be strengthened to ensure offenders cannot control access to a pet and ensure pets are not left with abusers. Police would be required to record the presence of pets in a family violence situation and receive clear operational guidance around removing pets to a safe place if the animal is at risk of harm.

**Why:** This party says that previous policy directions have required that public agencies should allocate services based on individual need and value, rather than race. *Topics: education, incomes-and-employment, schools, prices · Summary: policy.nz*

**Statement:** Limit the number of branded items in school uniforms to reduce costs

### Count carbon dioxide and methane differently under emissions targets (POL54667)

*Topics: environment, economy, emissions-reduction, agriculture, climate-adaptation · Summary: policy.nz*

**Statement:** Count carbon dioxide and methane differently under emissions targets

**Why:** This party says that carbon dioxide and methane both contribute to global heating. Carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere longer than methane, which is largely produced by the dairy and sheep industries.

**How:** This party would rewrite NZ's Nationally Determined Contributions plan, which is required by the Paris Agreement. It would differentiate between the emissions caused by methane and carbon dioxide so that methane emissions do not have to be reduced by the same degree as carbon emissions. Carbon dioxide emissions would be reduced while methane levels could continue at current levels.

**Statement:** Require a minimum three-year sentence for anyone convicted of burglary three times

**Statement:** Recognise introduced game species in law

**Why:** This party says that game animals on NZ's conservation land are treated as pests which should be killed. However, these animals are valuable to many rural communities and hunters and should be treated as natural resources instead. Hunters can strike a balance between removing game animals to protect the natural environment and ensuring there are enough game for the future.

**How:** This party would change legislation to designate game animals and birds as natural resources rather than pests. Herds of New Zealand deer, which hunters appreciate, would be designated as specific "Herds of Special Interest" for protection. The whitetail deer on Stewart Island would be given this designation.

**Statement:** Scale back the use and effect of Treaty principles in legislation

**Why:** This party says that, to protect democratic majority rule, judges cannot be allowed to enable Treaty principles to go beyond what Parliament intended. Greater clarity in legislation and removing Treaty considerations would provide greater protection of individual property rights and prevent ethnicity-based equity measures.

### Exclude purely spiritual and religious effects from infrastructure planning law (POL55191)

*Topics: te-ao-maori, transport-and-infrastructure, te-reo-maori-and-culture, infrastructure-funding-and-planning · Summary: policy.nz*

**Statement:** Exclude purely spiritual and religious effects from infrastructure planning law

**Why:** This party says that spiritual beliefs, particularly those that come from Te Ao Māori, should not be used as the basis for assessing an infrastructure project's viability. It says that planning law should regulate effects that can be identified, measured and tested, and protect rights recognised by law. It should not require planners, councils or judges to rule on spiritual or religious beliefs.

**How:** This party would exclude purely spiritual and religious effects. It would legislate that a religious or spiritual belief, or a claim of spiritual harm, could not on its own be treated as an adverse effect or justify refusing or restricting consent, requesting further information, or imposing a consent condition. The rule would apply equally to all religions and belief systems and use the test already applied under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act. It would also ban compulsory spiritual observances. No consent or permit could require anyone to perform, take part in, arrange or fund a prayer, karakia, blessing or other religious observance. Anyone who wants to do these things voluntarily could still do so.

# Labour Party: 2026 election policies

Every 2026 election policy of the New Zealand Labour Party that this archive could find, with summaries and links to the **full verbatim text** of every source page.

- **126 policies** in total: **76** listed by [policy.nz](https://policy.nz) (summaries by policy.nz, marked *policy.nz*) and **50** more found on labour.org.nz that policy.nz does not list separately (summaries written for this archive, marked *archive*).
- **138 full-text source documents** in [`documents/`](documents/): Labour's policy pages, PDFs, press releases and speeches on labour.org.nz, plus Scoop, RNZ and TVNZ pages that policy.nz cited. All were fetched from the original URLs (web.archive.org links in policy.nz were mapped back to the original pages) on **23 October 2026**. Text is verbatim; only the markup was turned into Markdown. Six policy PDFs (factsheets and policy documents linked from Labour pages) are also included as extracted text, and the PDFs themselves are kept in `raw/party-docs/labour/pdf/`.
- Structured data: [`policies.json`](policies.json). Scripts: `tools/policies_labour_fetch.py`, `tools/policies_labour_extract.py`, `tools/policies_labour_build.py`.
- How completeness was checked: every policy card on Labour's policy hub ([labour.org.nz/policy](https://www.labour.org.nz/policy)) and every page linked from it was captured. labour.org.nz has no sitemap.xml (it returns 404), so the list of all ~820 news items in the site's news menu was used instead: the ~300 most recent titles (roughly August 2025 to 22 October 2026) were read one by one and older ones were searched by keyword, and every release that announced a commitment was captured. Releases that only attack other parties, or report member's bills that have already passed, are not counted as policies.
- Each *archive* summary is a neutral restatement of what the linked Labour text says. Costings are Labour's own figures; none are independent estimates. Where sources disagree, this is noted.

## Headline commitments

These are the policy cards on Labour's [policy hub](https://www.labour.org.nz/policy), in Labour's order. Each description is Labour's own text (full page: [documents/policy.md](documents/policy.md)).

- **$20 Fare Cap**: $20 a week is the most you'll pay to get around by bus or train under Labour. In place by 1 July 2027.
- **Free Doctor's Visits**: Three free doctor's visits a year for everyone. Delivered with Labour's new Medicard.
- **Free Prescriptions**: Labour will remove the $5 fee on prescriptions to make them free for everyone. From 1 July 2027.
- **Free Maternity Scans**: Labour will make maternity scans free, everywhere in New Zealand with the Medicard. From July 2028.
- **Free Cervical Screening**: With Labour's Medicard, cervical screening will be free for ages 25-69. From 1 October 2027.
- **ED Recovery Plan**: Free GP visits, free prescriptions, more nurses and faster emergency care to ease pressure on emergency departments.
- **Family Doctor Loan Scheme**: Labour's Family Doctor Loan Scheme supports local GPs to buy into practices and stay in their communities. From 1 July 2027.
- **New Zealand Future Fund**: Backing New Zealand's potential and investing in a future made in New Zealand.
- **Capital Gains Tax**: A simple, targeted 28% tax on profit from selling investment property after 1 July 2027. Nine in 10 New Zealanders won't pay it.
- **Apprenticeship Boost**: Labour will support more tradies with extended employer payments, a $1,000 toolbox grant, and five new trades covered. From 1 July 2027.
- **SolarSaver**: Labour's SolarSaver is a fully-funded programme to help homeowners, renters and communities get solar without the upfront cost.
- **Small Business Action Plan**: Getting small business owners paid sooner, easier ways to invest, and less paperwork.
- **Small Business First**: A fair shot at work and less time dealing with the government.
- **Fiscal Plan**: Balance the books, return to surplus by 2028/29, reduce net debt towards 20% of GDP, and keep government spending and revenue sustainable.
- **AI in New Zealand's Interests**: Protect what matters, unlock our potential, and lead on our own terms with a new Office of AI and a framework to recognise and pay creators when AI uses their work.
- **Backing Māori into Skilled Work**: Māori-led training that helps more whānau Māori gain skills and move into good, well-paid work.
- **Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee**: Every eligible New Zealand-trained graduate nurse will be offered a job in our health system, from 2027.
- **Strengthening KiwiSaver**: Compulsory employer contributions rising to 6% by 2032, plus support during parental leave and over-65s.
- **Banning Price Gouging**: Making it illegal for big companies to overcharge for essentials.
- **Fairer Grocery Prices**: More competition, more choice, fairer prices by breaking open the supermarket duopoly's grip on wholesale supply.
- **Start Work Now**: Building homes, fixing schools and repairing hospitals - getting Kiwis back on the tools and nearly 30,000 apprentices into work.
- **Cutting Student Debt**: A 10% cut to eligible student loan balances, with small balances under $2,000 written off completely.
- **A Fair Go For Families**: No hidden fees. No traps. No rip-offs. Banning junk insurance and making cancelling as easy as signing up.
- **Pay Equity**: Restoring pay equity legislation and giving an immediate pay rise to care and support workers.
- **A Fair Go For Drivers**: Fairer fuel pricing, a right to repair law for cars, and a fairer deal at the car yard.
- **Fuel Tax Freeze**: Labour will freeze fuel excise tax for three years, saving an average family $520 a year by 2030.
- **Banking for Everyone**: Opening up banking competition, backing Kiwi fintech with a new digital banking licence, and keeping Kiwibank 100% New Zealand-owned.
- **A Better Deal When You Fly**: Real prices upfront, automatic refunds when things go wrong, and more airlines competing for your business.
- **Cutting Back-to-School Costs**: Cheaper uniforms, healthy school lunches back from Term 1 2028, rural school buses restored, and lower transport costs.
- **Keeping Kids off Screens**: Kids being kids for longer: sport grants, after-school activities, clearer screen rules in schools and support for parents.
- **Safer Online**: Basic rules for big tech: no social media for under-16s, more control over your feed, and a Digital Duty of Care.

## Fiscal plan and costings

Labour published its Fiscal Plan on 4 October 2026 ([labour.org.nz/fiscal-plan](https://www.labour.org.nz/fiscal-plan), full text: [documents/fiscal-plan.md](documents/fiscal-plan.md)). Its earlier fiscal strategy page is at [documents/fiscal-strategy.md](documents/fiscal-strategy.md). The key facts as Labour states them:

- Every election commitment is fully costed and fully funded, independently reviewed by Hall Chadwick
- Books return to an OBEGAL surplus in 2028/29
- Net debt down towards 20% of GDP over time
- Operating allowance held at $2.4 billion per Budget, as set at Budget 2026
- $12 billion in future capital allowances; Labour's commitments use $4.1 billion, leaving almost $8 billion unallocated
- $15.5 billion of additional health funding over the forecast period

Capital commitments (from the Fiscal Plan page):

Labour's announced capital commitments fit comfortably within the $12 billion of future capital allowances, leaving almost $8 billion unallocated.

| Commitment | Capital funding |
| --- | --- |
| New Zealand Future Fund | $200 million |
| Student loan write-off | $420 million |
| Hospitals | $200 million |
| Schools | $400 million |
| Kainga Ora housing (over four years) | $2.9 billion |
| Ratepayer Assistance Scheme solar expenditure | $7 million |

Costings listed on Labour's policy hub FAQ ("How are Labour's policies being funded?"), verbatim:

- free prescriptions: $74.5 million a year
- free maternity scans: $28.6 million a year
- free cervical screening: $21.6 million a year
- Apprenticeship Boost: an average of $56.5 million a year over four years
- SolarSaver: $160 million over four years
- Backing Māori into Skilled Work: $21 million a year
- the Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee: $525 million
- the Small Business Action Plan: $1.56 billion over four years, funded by refocusing Investment Boost
- Start Work Now: around $450 million for schools, $200 million for hospitals and $2.9 billion in capital for housing
- Pay equity is funded within Labour's Fiscal Plan, with future settlements funded through future Budgets as agreements are reached.
- The $950 million Crown guarantee for the Community Housing Funding Agency would only be called on in the unlikely event of a default.

> Note on timing: policy.nz (citing Labour's August fiscal strategy page) gives the OBEGAL surplus year as 2029/30. Labour's Fiscal Plan of 4 October 2026 says 2028/29.

## Health

### Remove $5 charge for prescriptions

`POL54665` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Incomes & employment

**Why:** This party says that that last year, 155,000 New Zealanders didn't collect medicine they had been prescribed because they couldn't afford it. Not receiving treatments mean that health problems are exacerbated, and research shows that people who skip medication are more likely to end up in hospital. Making prescriptions free is an upfront cost for the government which removes pressure on the health system.

**How:** This party would remove the $5 fee for prescriptions of funded medication. This would apply to anyone who is entitled to free healthcare in New Zealand, instead of just people under age 14 and over age 65 and those with Community Services Cards. This would cost $74.5m a year, funded by a capital gains tax. This party estimates that this policy would cost $74.5 m a year.

**Costing (as stated):** This would cost $74.5m a year, funded by a capital gains tax. This party estimates that this policy would cost $74.5 m a year.

**Full text:** ['Free Prescriptions Under Labour', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)](documents/prescriptions.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/prescriptions)); [Affordable Healthcare - NZ Labour's Medicard Plan](documents/affordable-healthcare.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/affordable-healthcare))

### Make up to three GP visits a year free

`POL54669` · summary: *policy.nz*

**Why:** This party says that many New Zealanders have to choose between medical care and other essentials like food. Some general practices charge nearly $100 per visit. Under the "Medicard" policy programme, anyone eligible for funded healthcare could go to the GP for free at least three times a year. This would be paid for by a capital gains tax.

**How:** This party would cover three visits a year to a doctor or nurse at the GP clinic where people are enrolled. Already free services like immunisations would not count towards the three-visit total. The "Medicard" card and app would link visits to people's National Health Index number. The three free visits are for each year and do not accumulate and roll over into the next year. This party estimates that this policy would cost $393.3 million in 2027/28, rising to around $553 million a year once fully in place.

**Costing (as stated):** This party estimates that this policy would cost $393.3 million in 2027/28, rising to around $553 million a year once fully in place.

**Full text:** ['Free Doctor's Visits with the Medicard', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)](documents/medicard.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/medicard)); [Affordable Healthcare - NZ Labour's Medicard Plan](documents/affordable-healthcare.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/affordable-healthcare)); [Labour's ED Recovery Plan](documents/ed-recovery-plan.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/ed-recovery-plan)); [Labour: Free doctor's visits (Medicard) - PDF](documents/pdf-labour-free-doctors-visits.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/media/vtbneplb/labour-free-doctors-visits.pdf))

### Ensure all referred maternity scans are free

`POL54686` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Community & inclusion

**Why:** This party says that that pregnant people should not have to worry about money to know their baby is healthy, with each scan currently costing an average $90. No mum would have to skip a scan because they can't afford it.

**How:** This party would make every referred maternity scan by a doctor, midwife or specialist free in NZ. All a pregnant person would need is a Medicard. ### Remove rough sleepers from "Move On" bill

`POL54889` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Law, justice & government

**Why:** This party says that the current 'Move On' bill criminalises people for sleeping rough when they have no other option. ## Environment

### Provide loans for people to purchase solar set-ups for their homes

`POL54717` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Housing, Transport & infrastructure

**Why:** This party says that says that power bills have risen by 20 percent in the last two years. **How:** This party would create a SolarSaver fund, which includes two new Government-backed, long-term, low-interest finance options. The first loan is a Lines company loan, where you borrow through your local lines company to cover the cost of solar and a battery, repaid via your power bill. The second loan is a Ratepayer Assistance Scheme, a low-interest loan attached to your home covering solar, batteries and other home electrification. The party would also amend power regulations so renters can use plug-in solar panels, with a subsidy available to cover the cost of purchase. Funding would come from the Government's Gas Security Fund. This party estimates that this policy would cost $160 million over four years.

**Costing (as stated):** This party estimates that this policy would cost $160 million over four years.

### Make Kiwisaver more flexible for workers

`POL54985` · summary: *policy.nz*

**Why:** This party says that Kiwisaver is crucial to building a secure future and a key source of investment for the economy. However, more than a million working-age KiwiSaver members are not contributing at all, while 83,400 are on a savings suspension. This party would take the government's proposed Kiwisaver plan and make it more flexible for workers, particularly those under financial pressure.

**How:** This party would make KiwiSaver more flexible and therefore more attractive for Kiwis to save. It would make employer contributions compulsory and lift them to 6 percent by 2032. **How:** This party would adjust legislation to address price gouging and give the Commerce Commission to new powers investigate what dominant companies are charging and take them to court. `POL55306` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Economy

**Why:** This party says that Māori unemployment has increased to nearly 11% and the Māori economy has gone backwards. However, Māori businesses have demonstrated that they can deliver. Overseas, indigenous minority-owned businesses have risen significantly and this has improved socio-economic conditions for targeted groups.

**How:** This party would reinstate its Progressive Procurement policy, which would initially allocate 5% of government procurement contracts to Māori businesses.. This has proven sustainable in the past and would equate to about $900m worth of contracts, injecting capital into Māori businesses and supporting wider growth.

**Full text:** ['Labour will back Māori business and grow the Māori economy', 15 October 2026 (accessed 16 October 2026)](documents/release-labour-will-back-maori-businesses-and-grow-the-maori-economy.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/release-labour-will-back-maori-businesses-and-grow-the-maori-economy/)); [Backing Māori Businesses](documents/backing-maori-businesses.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/backing-maori-businesses))

## Defence & foreign affairs

### Increase foreign aid to 0.7 percent of GDP

`POL55129` · summary: *policy.nz*

**Why:** This party says that NZ needs to have an independent foreign policy, focused on Pacific partners. The country needs friendship and allies with close partners, particularly in Australia and the Pacific, in uncertain times.

**How:** This party would progressively increase international aid to 0.7 percent of GDP, as fiscal limitations allow. There is no specific time limit for this policy.

**Note:** policy.nz says 0.7% of GDP; Labour's Foreign Affairs page says "towards 0.7% of GNI as fiscal conditions allow".

**Full text:** ['Labour's foreign policy', 23 September 2026 (accessed 23 September 2026)](documents/speech-labours-foreign-policy.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/speech-labours-foreign-policy/)); [Foreign Affairs](documents/foreign-affairs.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/foreign-affairs))

### Work towards a Pacific agreement on climate mitigation

`POL55130` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Environment

**Why:** This party says that the Pacific is NZ's neighbourhood, and NZ is a Pacific country. These relationships are especially important as NZ is going to host the Pacific Islands Forum in 2027. Climate change and economic development are major challenges in this region, and NZ needs to support neighbouring countries with these challenges.

**How:** This party would work towards a Pacific agreement on climate mitigation, adaptation and displacement. It would specifically focus on Tuvalu and Kiribati on long-term plans for climate adaptation and possible resettlement.

**Full text:** ['Labour's foreign policy', 23 September 2026 (accessed 23 September 2026)](documents/speech-labours-foreign-policy.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/speech-labours-foreign-policy/)); ['NZ: An independent voice in the world', 23 September 2026 (accessed 23 September 2026)](documents/speech-new-zealand-an-independent-voice-in-the-world.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/speech-new-zealand-an-independent-voice-in-the-world/)); [Foreign Affairs](documents/foreign-affairs.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/foreign-affairs))

### Recognise the state of Palestine

`POL55131` · summary: *policy.nz*

**Why:** This party says that NZ has a reputation as an honest and independent country which defends international law. When human rights abuses and war create genocide and ethnic cleansing, NZ must have the moral clarity to speak up, specifically regarding the situation in Palestine.

**How:** This party would recognise the state of Palestine at the UN and place economic sanctions on Israel. It would ensure that the ACC and NZ Super Funds are divested from holdings in the Palestinian occupied territories, according to the list prepared by the UN. It would support South Africa at its case at the International Court of Justice, saying that Israel is breaching the Genocide Convention.

**Full text:** ['Labour's foreign policy', 23 September 2026 (accessed 23 September 2026)](documents/speech-labours-foreign-policy.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/speech-labours-foreign-policy/)); [Foreign Affairs](documents/foreign-affairs.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/foreign-affairs))

### Develop new trade markets around the world

`POL55133` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Economy

**Why:** This party says that the world is more uncertain and more competitive than at any time in recent memory, and old alliances and assumptions are under real strain. It is possible to trade as well as disagree with a country. Public support for globalisations is decreasing, but the answer is agreements with other markets, not tariffs.

**How:** This party would continue to pursue trade agreements, especially with new markets in Africa and South America. It would prioritise relationships with ASEAN countries, the EU and Canada. It would make it easier to move money and data across the Pacific.

**Full text:** ['Labour's foreign policy', 23 September 2026 (accessed 23 September 2026)](documents/speech-labours-foreign-policy.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/speech-labours-foreign-policy/)); [Foreign Affairs](documents/foreign-affairs.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/foreign-affairs))

### Continue support for the Paris Agreement, Antarctic Treaty and other international institutions

`POL55134` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Environment

**Why:** This party says that climate change, conflict and migration do not stop at borders, and NZ has a responsibility to the world. While institutions like the UN, WTO, International Court of Justice and International Criminal Court are imperfect, they need continued support to be reformed rather than abandoned. As a small country, NZ needs to do its part to work on goals like the Paris agreement and the care of Antarctica.

**How:** This party would support and retain membership of the UN, World Trade Organisation, International Court of Justice and International Criminal Court. It would continue to fulfil the responsibilities and requirements of the Paris Agreement and Antarctic Treaty and advocate for international scientific cooperation. It would support the country of Ukraine in its war against Russia.

**Full text:** ['NZ: An independent voice in the world', 23 September 2026 (accessed 23 September 2026)](documents/speech-new-zealand-an-independent-voice-in-the-world.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/speech-new-zealand-an-independent-voice-in-the-world/)); ['Labour's foreign policy', 23 September 2026 (accessed 23 September 2026)](documents/speech-labours-foreign-policy.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/speech-labours-foreign-policy/)); ['Labour to accelerate climate action', 8 September 2026 (accessed 08 September 2026)](documents/release-labour-to-accelerate-climate-action.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/release-labour-to-accelerate-climate-action/)); [Foreign Affairs](documents/foreign-affairs.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/foreign-affairs)); [Fixing the Emissions Trading Scheme](documents/fixing-the-ets.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/fixing-the-ets))

### Expand visa-waiver access for Pacific Island Forum nations

`POL55215` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Community & inclusion

**Why:** This party says that it often falls on Pasifika families in NZ to sponsor a visit from loved ones from the islands, but for cost or other reasons, they may be unable to secure a visa. This party says NZ values its Pacific community and should reduce the barriers for them to connect with family.

**How:** This party would expand visa-waiver access to citizens from the Pacific Islands Forum nations.

**Full text:** ['Release: Labour will expand visa-waiver travel to Pacific citizens', 17 September 2026 (accessed 23 September 2026)](documents/release-labour-will-expand-visa-waiver-travel-to-pacific-citizens.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/release-labour-will-expand-visa-waiver-travel-to-pacific-citizens/)); [Immigration](documents/immigration.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/immigration)); [Foreign Affairs](documents/foreign-affairs.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/foreign-affairs))

### Reform the UN Charter and back the WHO

`LAB-A35` · summary: *archive*

**Summary:** Labour would support reviewing and "maturing" the UN Charter, support the World Health Organization and adopt the updated WHO health regulations.

**Full text:** [Foreign Affairs](documents/foreign-affairs.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/foreign-affairs))

### Push for a ban on lethal autonomous weapons and parliamentary scrutiny of military deployments

`LAB-A36` · summary: *archive*

## Media, culture & recreation

### Support a social media ban for under-16s to go through to select committee

`POL54753` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Economy, Community & inclusion, Te ao Māori

**Why:** This party says that it is important to help parents keep their children safe from online harm, but any law would need to be fit for purpose.

**How:** This party would support the bill through its first reading and see it go to select committee before the election.

**Full text:** ['Labour clears way for social media bill to go to select committee', 25 August 2026 (accessed 26 August 2026)](documents/release-labour-clears-way-for-social-media-bill-to-go-to-select-committee.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/release-labour-clears-way-for-social-media-bill-to-go-to-select-committee/)); [Safer Online](documents/safer-online.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/safer-online))

### Tighten digital regulation, especially around deepfakes, children and social media

`POL55312` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Education, Economy, Community & inclusion

**Why:** This party says that smart phones are one of the parenting challenges of our time. Tech companies have too much power over what we see and fake images are harder to spot. Many parents worry about what their children are seeing or if they are being bullied. More responsibility should be placed on the companies making money from these platforms.

**How:** This party would introduce more digital regulation to Parliament within the first 100 days, including no social media accounts for under-16s. Social media companies would be legally responsible for policing this, and a new digital duty of care will be introduced with stronger privacy and other protections for those under 18. Other action would include more control for users over their feeds, and stronger rules around deepfakes and non-consensual sexual images. An independent digital regulator will be created, with powers to take action against companies that break the rules.

### Provide more support for children's sports and hobbies

`POL55313` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Education, Economy, Community & inclusion

**Why:** This party says that parents and schools need help to keep kids safer online, keep them active and prevent screen addiction. Technology has its place, but at present it's a dominant force in children's lives while sport, hobbies and other after-school activities are out of reach for many families.

**How:** This party would boost funding for after school sport and activities with an extra $4m for Tū Manawa Active Aotearoa and $12m over four years for the Active Me - Kia Tū programme which supports families with sports registration, uniforms and equipment. This is part of a wider set of policies around AI and digital use which includes clear expectations around screentime in school and a continuation of the ban on mobile phones in class.
