# National Party — 2026 election policies

Every 2026 general-election policy of the New Zealand National Party (Te Rōpū Nāhinara) that this archive could find, with a short summary of each and links to the **full verbatim text** of National's own policy documents, web pages and press releases.

- **159 policies**: 126 from [policy.nz](https://policy.nz) (the Why/How summaries are policy.nz's neutral summaries) plus 33 further commitments found in National's own documents that policy.nz does not list separately (summaries written by this archive, marked `NAT-ARC-xx`).
- **136 source documents** in [`documents/`](documents/): 36 PDF policy documents, 40 policy pages from national.org.nz, 57 National Party press releases/speeches, and 3 third-party pages cited by policy.nz (Beehive, RNZ).
- Retrieved **2026-10-23** directly from national.org.nz / assets.national.org.nz (policy hub: <https://www.national.org.nz/policies>), beehive.govt.nz and rnz.co.nz. Original PDFs and HTML are kept in `raw/party-docs/national/`. Scripts: `tools/policies_national_*.py`.
- Policy statements, Why/How summaries and topics for `POL…` entries come from policy.nz (`raw/policy.nz/parties/national-party.json`). Costings are shown only where National or policy.nz states one.
- National is the senior party in the current (2023–2026) coalition Government, so some documents mix new election promises with descriptions of what the Government has already done. Entries here are the forward-looking commitments.

## Contents

- [Key commitments / headline policies](#key-commitments--headline-policies)
- [Costings & fiscal plan](#costings--fiscal-plan)
- Policies by topic:
  - [Economy](#economy) (46)
  - [Incomes & employment](#incomes--employment) (12)
  - [Health](#health) (14)
  - [Education](#education) (19)
  - [Housing](#housing) (4)
  - [Transport & infrastructure](#transport--infrastructure) (29)
  - [Environment](#environment) (14)
  - [Law, justice & government](#law-justice--government) (9)
  - [Community & inclusion](#community--inclusion) (8)
  - [Migration](#migration) (1)
  - [Defence & foreign affairs](#defence--foreign-affairs) (2)
  - [Media, culture & recreation](#media-culture--recreation) (1)
- [All source documents](#all-source-documents)

## Key commitments / headline policies

National's campaign slogan is “Fixing the Basics. Building the Future.” Its central promises, as set out on its policy hub, “Our Plan” page and campaign launch, are:

- No new taxes in the next term (including no capital gains tax), and keep Investment Boost — [POL54733](#introduce-no-new-taxes-in-the-next-term-of-government), [NAT-ARC-20](#keep-investment-boost)
- Return to surplus in 2028/29, keep net core Crown debt below 40% of GDP, spending towards 30% of GDP (Budget Responsibility Rules) — [POL54725](#create-a-government-surplus-by-202829), [POL54726](#keep-government-debt-below-40-percent-of-gdp), [POL54727](#keep-crown-expenditure-close-to-30-per-cent-of-gdp)
- Make KiwiSaver compulsory from 1 July 2028 (combined contributions rising to 12% by 2032), $1,500 “Baby Boost” and auto-enrolment at birth, KiwiSaver top-up during paid parental leave, employer contributions for over-65s — [POL54734](#enrol-new-zealand-citizens-in-kiwisaver-at-birth)
- Extend paid parental leave from 26 to 30 weeks by 2029 — [POL54715](#increase-paid-parental-leave-to-30-weeks-by-2029)
- Widen 5% deposit First Home Loans (income cap raised to $300,000) — [POL54918](#raise-the-income-threshold-for-people-who-can-pay-a-lower-deposit-for-their-first-home)
- Cut the student loan repayment rate from 12% to 10% and get tougher on overseas defaulters — [POL54813](#reduce-the-student-loan-repayment-rate-to-10-percent), [POL54814](#fund-further-enforcement-and-create-harsher-penalties-for-overseas-based-student-loan-holders)
- A further $604m for Pharmac, bowel screening from age 50, breast screening to 74, free cervical screening 25–69 — [POL55205](#increase-funding-for-pharmacs-medicines-budget), [POL55208](#lower-the-free-bowel-screening-age-to-50-by-2029), [POL55209](#extend-free-breast-screening-extension-to-age-74-by-2029), [POL55211](#deliver-free-cervical-screening-for-all-women-aged-25-to-69)
- Pursue structural separation of Foodstuffs into two competing nationwide grocery groups (subject to Commerce Commission assessment) — [POL55014](#separate-the-foodstuffs-business-into-two-nationwide-cooperatives)
- Cap council rate rises (2–4%) — [POL54817](#instruct-councils-to-keep-annual-rate-increases-between-2-and-4-percent)
- Firmer welfare: work support for 30,000 jobseekers, lower rate after two years, drug testing, five-year residency rule — [POL55226](#provide-targeted-work-support-to-30000-jobseekers), [POL55227](#reduce-benefit-payments-for-people-receiving-support-for-more-than-2-years), [POL55228](#introduce-drug-testing-for-people-receiving-benefits), [POL55230](#change-entitlements-for-benefits-for-new-nz-residents-to-5-years)
- Replace NCEA; keep students at school until end of Year 11; no screens in ECE; ban under-16s from social media — [POL55174](#replace-ncea-with-a-different-grading-system), [POL55259](#require-students-to-finish-year-11-before-leaving-school), [POL55050](#limit-the-use-of-screens-in-school-for-primary-aged-and-younger-children), [POL54815](#ban-under-16-year-olds-from-social-media)
- Big transport builds: Belfast–Pegasus/Woodend Bypass ($800m), Mill Road Stage One ($1.75b), next Roads of National Significance — [POL55201](#fund-800-million-christchurch-northern-motorway-extension), [NAT-ARC-01](#fund-construction-of-mill-road-stage-one-manukau-to-alfriston-in-south-auckland), [POL55177](#complete-construction-on-the-next-set-of-roads-of-national-significance)
- Energy: Home Energy Fund loans for solar/batteries, consent-free rooftop solar, Electrify NZ 2.0 market changes — [POL54922](#offer-government-backed-long-term-loans-for-home-batteries-and-solar-installations), [POL54923](#allow-rooftop-solar-and-battery-installation-without-a-consent), [POL55183](#legislate-affordability-as-a-concern-of-the-electricity-authority)
- Double exports by 2034 and pursue trade deals with “the next billion customers” — [POL54712](#double-nzs-export-earnings-by-2034), [POL54711](#pursue-trade-deals-with-european-south-american-asian-and-african-countries)
- Law and order: dedicated Auckland transport police, remove right to silence where a child is murdered, “yes means yes” consent law, end good-character discounts for sexual offending — [POL54978](#create-a-dedicated-police-team-for-auckland-public-transport), [POL55322](#remove-the-right-to-silence-in-criminal-cases-where-a-child-has-been-murdered), [POL54925](#specify-that-an-active-yes-is-required-in-laws-around-sexual-consent), [POL54926](#prevent-good-character-from-being-a-mitigating-factor-in-sentencing-for-sexual-offending)

National published a **Fiscal Plan** ([full text](documents/pdf-nationals-fiscal-plan.md); [web page](documents/policy-nationals-fiscal-plan.md)) and **Budget Responsibility Rules** ([full text](documents/pdf-nationals-budget-responsibility-rules.md)). In summary (all figures are National's own):

## Economy

#### Invest $50m in roads and rail lines to create a transport hub in Rolleston

`POL54693` · topics: economy, transport-and-infrastructure, regional-development, rail-transport, cars-and-roads, economic-development-and-industry, infrastructure-funding-and-planning, agriculture · summary: policy.nz

- **Why:** This party says that Rolleston is a well-placed hub for moving goods around, as it is on State Highway 1, the main southern train line, and connected by road and rail to the West Coast. Because many agricultural goods are moved through this area, making it easier to move goods between trains and trucks will increase efficiency and economic opportunity for producers in this area.
- **How:** This party would invest $50m in a road and rail "intermodal hub" in Rolleston. This funding would be dependent on the result of a business case, where private freight companies and customers would also invest in the hub. It would only go ahead with a mix of public and private funding. This party estimates that this policy would cost $50m.
- **Costing:** This party estimates that this policy would cost $50m.

#### Change the policy settings for farmers leasing high country land from the Crown

`POL54696` · topics: economy, environment, agriculture, conservation · summary: policy.nz

- **Why:** This party says that the Crown owns 1.2 million hectares of land through the South Island, which is leased to farmers for pastoral grazing. Much of this land is at higher elevations. Farmers need certainty about which kinds of activities they can do on this land without requiring consent. Giving farmers other income sources on this land, like beekeeping or horticulture, would provide farmers with the confidence to invest and diversify.

The First Home Loan scheme has operated since 2003, allowing people to purchase their first homes with a 5% deposit, instead of a standard 20% deposit. - **Why:** This party says that New Zealand has over 1900 seamounts (mountains and hills on the ocean floor which often have more biodiversity) in its Exclusive Economic Zone (the area of ocean which a country has the right to resources within). `POL54925` · topics: law-justice-and-government, criminal-justice · summary: policy.nz

- **Why:** This party says that NZ law does not define what consent is, but instead says what consent is not. ## Media, culture & recreation

#### Rule out a licence for recreational sea fishing

`POL55263` · topics: media-culture-and-recreation, economy, sports-and-recreation, fisheries, tourism · summary: policy.nz

- **Why:** This party says that at least 600,000 New Zealanders go fishing occasionally, and recreational fish provides food and enjoyment, as well as supporting the business of charter boat tourism for fishing access. Fish stocks need to be maintained for recreational users, but fishing for food is a right and should not require a licence. This party says that honorary Fisheries Officers, who do enforcement work on a voluntary basis, could be doing more of the work of fisheries enforcement.
- **How:** This party would ensure that no licence is required for sea fishing. It would ban the commercial sale of marlin, so hunting this fish can continue to be a sport. Enforcement and fines for people who do not obey catch limits would be increased, and part of this enforcement would be carried out by increasing the number of Honorary Fisheries Officers to 200 around the country. There would be some instant fines for people who catch more than the limit of fish.

# Chris Hipkins | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Current MP, standing in 2026 | | **Born** | 1978-09-05 — Hutt Valley, New Zealand | | **Electorate(s) held** | Rimutaka, Remutaka | | **Parliaments** | 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54 | | **First elected** | 2008 | | **2026 candidacy** | Remutaka · list #1 | | **Key roles** | Labour shadow cabinet #1 (as of 11 Mar 2026): Leader of the Opposition; Spokesperson for Ministerial Services; Spokesperson for National Security and Intelligence
41st Leader of the Opposition (2023–)
41st Prime Minister of New Zealand (2023)
18th Leader of the Labour Party (2023–)
Minister of National Security and Intelligence (2023)
Leader of the House (2017–2023) | | **Wikipedia** | [Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hipkins) | ## Current status Hipkins is Leader of the Opposition and Labour leader heading into the 7 November 2026 general election, in which he is standing again in Remutaka and is first on Labour's list ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)). Labour's caucus confirmed him as leader after the 2023 defeat on 7 November 2023 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/501872/labour-votes-to-keep-chris-hipkins-as-leader-carmel-sepuloni-takes-over-as-deputy)). In October 2025 he announced that Labour would campaign on a narrow 28% capital gains tax on property sales (excluding the family home and farms) to fund three free doctor's visits a year, and ruled out a wealth tax ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/577021/labour-to-campaign-on-narrow-capital-gains-tax-no-wealth-tax)). ## Biography Christopher John Hipkins was born on 5 September 1978 in the Hutt Valley, the son of Doug and Rosemary Hipkins ([Parliament maiden statement](https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/hansard-debates/rhr/document/49HansS_20081216_00001004/hipkins-chris-maiden-statements); [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/482831/chris-hipkins-from-head-boy-to-prime-minister)). He was head boy of Hutt Valley Memorial College in 1996 and studied political science and criminology at Victoria University of Wellington (BA), where he was students' association president in 2000 and 2001 ([Beehive biography](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/minister/biography/chris-hipkins)). As a first-year student in 1997 he was among protesters arrested at Parliament over the Tertiary Review green paper; a decade later the protesters received an apology and compensation after a court found the arrests unjustified ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/dominion-post/news/local-papers/hutt-news/2595536/Parliament-to-say-sorry-to-protestors)). Before entering Parliament he was a policy adviser at the Industry Training Federation, a training manager at Todd Energy, and an adviser to ministers Trevor Mallard and Prime Minister Helen Clark ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/chris-hipkins-from-hutt-valley-boy-to-quiet-coup-for-pm-audrey-young-reports/ET4JZSI5PVCKBDDHRCLYVQ3CHI/)). He married Jade in 2020; they separated in 2022 and have two children. In 2018 he took extended paternity leave, one of the first senior male cabinet ministers to do so. His relationship with Toni Grace became public on election night 2023 and he announced their engagement in November 2025 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/labour-leader-chris-hipkins-reveals-engagement-to-partner-toni-grace/32RDT6TDINBDBCJ3XR2Z23OIAQ/)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2008–2011 | Rimutaka | 47 | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | Rimutaka | 30 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Rimutaka | 9 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Rimutaka | 7 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Remutaka | 6 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–present | Remutaka | 1 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 41st Leader of the Opposition | 27 November 2023 | present | Christopher Luxon | | 41st Prime Minister of New Zealand | 25 January 2023 | 27 November 2023 | | | 18th Leader of the Labour Party | 22 January 2023 | present | | | Minister of National Security and Intelligence | 25 January 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Himself | | Leader of the House | 26 October 2017 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister of Education | 26 October 2017 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister of Public Service | 26 October 2017 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister of Police | 14 June 2022 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister for COVID-19 Response | 6 November 2020 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister of Health | 2 July 2020 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Opposition portfolios (as of 11 March 2026) Rank 1 in Chris Hipkins' shadow cabinet: - Leader of the Opposition - Spokesperson for Ministerial Services - Spokesperson for National Security and Intelligence _Source: [Shadow Cabinet of Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Chris_Hipkins), list as of 11 March 2026._ **Electorate.** Hipkins won the Labour-held Rimutaka seat (renamed Remutaka in 2020) in 2008 after Paul Swain retired, beating union official Paul Chalmers for the nomination. His majorities: 753 (2008), 3,286 (2011), 6,664 (2014), 8,609 (2017), 8,859 (2023); in 2020 he polled 20,497 votes (official results via [electionresults.govt.nz 2011](http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2011/electorate-43.html), [2014](http://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2014/electorate-44.html), [2017](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/electorate-details-44.html), [2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-42.html), [2023](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-42.html)). **Opposition, 2008–2017.** Spokesperson for internal affairs in his first term; under David Shearer he entered the shadow cabinet as education and state services spokesperson and became Labour's chief whip; he kept education under David Cunliffe, Andrew Little and Jacinda Ardern and was also shadow Leader of the House from 2014 ([Parliament profile](https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/members-of-parliament/hipkins-chris/)). **Minister, 2017–2023.** In the Sixth Labour Government he was Minister of Education and Leader of the House (26 Oct 2017 – 25 Jan 2023), Minister for the Public Service (2017–2023), Minister of Health (2 Jul – 6 Nov 2020, after David Clark resigned), Minister for COVID-19 Response (6 Nov 2020 – 14 Jun 2022) and Minister of Police (14 Jun 2022 – 25 Jan 2023), earning a reputation as the government's "fixer" ([The Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/21-01-2023/the-guy-just-lives-for-diy-what-to-expect-from-prime-minister-chris-hipkins); [DPMC ministerial list Nov 2020](https://dpmc.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2020-11/ministerial-list-2-nov-2020.pdf)). **Prime Minister, 2023.** After Jacinda Ardern resigned, Hipkins was the only nominee for the Labour leadership (21–22 January 2023) and was sworn in as the 41st Prime Minister on 25 January 2023, with Carmel Sepuloni as the first Pasifika deputy prime minister ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/chris-hipkins-sworn-in-as-prime-minister-carmel-sepuloni-as-deputy-jacinda-ardern-vacates-top-job/IERZGZV2BFAE5AWLNJHMMGHYQ4/)). He led Labour to defeat at the October 2023 election (26.91% of the party vote, 34 seats) and conceded on election night ([Electoral Commission](https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2023/official-results-for-the-2023-general-election/); [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/500185/election-2023-labour-s-chris-hipkins-concedes-congratulates-national-on-results)). He remained caretaker PM until Christopher Luxon was sworn in on 27 November 2023. **Opposition leader, 2023–present.** He took the ministerial services and national security & intelligence spokesperson roles in his shadow cabinet ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/503581/labour-party-leader-chris-hipkins-reveals-new-shadow-cabinet)) and in March 2025 reshuffled it and created an economic team led by Barbara Edmonds ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/544048/chris-hipkins-announces-new-labour-economic-team-tangi-utikere-promoted)). ## Record & notable actions - **Education (2017–2023):** legislated to stop new charter schools; all 12 existing charter schools became state-integrated or special-character schools by September 2018 ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2018/09/all-nz-charter-schools-now-approved-to-become-state-integrated.html)). Abolished National Standards and reviewed NCEA. Merged the 16 polytechnics and the industry training organisations into Te Pūkenga (from April 2020), a reform that by 2022 faced low enrolments, deficits and senior resignations ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/395722/government-confirms-major-overhaul-of-polytechnics-apprenticeships); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/waikato-times/300647698/minister-rules-out-te-pkenga-commissioner-at-this-time)). Declined Victoria University's proposed renaming to "University of Wellington" in 2018 ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/education/109441495/victoria-university-of-wellington-name-change-rejected-by-minister)). - **COVID-19 response (2020–2022):** introduced mask mandates on public transport, pre-departure testing, the My Vaccine Pass and the COVID-19 Response (Vaccinations) Legislation Act 2021 (vaccine-mandate framework) ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/456455/mandate-legislation-pushed-through-parliament-amid-fierce-opposition)); oversaw MIQ, including the January 2022 pause of the MIQ lottery ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/459786/government-postpones-next-miq-lottery-due-to-spike-of-omicron-cases-at-border)); announced in October 2022 the end of most COVID powers and a Royal Commission of Inquiry ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/476919/government-signals-covid-19-inquiry-in-the-works)). - **As Prime Minister (2023):** a "policy bonfire" scrapping or deferring the TVNZ–RNZ merger, the biofuel mandate, lowering the voting age to 16, the Clean Car Upgrade and much of the speed-reduction programme, and delaying social insurance and hate-speech law, with funds redirected to cost-of-living support ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/483875/watch-tvnz-rnz-merger-scrapped-income-insurance-and-hate-speech-laws-delayed); [1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/03/13/pms-policy-bonfire-voting-age-bill-transport-schemes-reprioritsed/)); led the response to the Auckland Anniversary floods and Cyclone Gabrielle; Budget 2023 removed $5 prescription fees, extended 20 hours ECE to two-year-olds and made public transport free for under-13s ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/490161/budget-2023-at-a-glance-what-you-need-to-know)); signed the NZ–EU free trade agreement on 9 July 2023 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/493457/new-zealand-signs-free-trade-deal-with-european-union-after-years-of-negotiations)); ruled out a capital gains or wealth tax for the 2023 term ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/493596/hipkins-rules-out-capital-gains-tax-wealth-tax-if-labour-re-elected)). - **In opposition:** called for a Gaza ceasefire (November 2023) and in September 2025 said New Zealand should recognise the situation in Gaza as genocide ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/573334/nz-govt-will-not-respond-on-latest-accusation-of-genocide-in-gaza)); in April 2026 committed Labour's votes to pass the NZ–India free trade agreement, which NZ First opposed ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/593185/chris-hipkins-announces-labour-will-back-india-free-trade-deal)). - **Conscience votes:** voted for the Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill in 2013 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/gay-marriage-how-mps-voted/WLPKK4734FBZEKJIDHBFO4MWFA/)). - **Member's bills:** Electricity (Renewable Preference) Amendment Bill (defeated at first reading, 2010); Education (Charter Schools Abolition) Amendment Bill (defeated at first reading, 2016) ([Parliament](https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/00DBHOH_BILL68842_1/education-charter-schools-abolition-amendment-bill)). ## Controversies - **Charlotte Bellis MIQ case (2022):** as COVID-19 Response Minister he publicly released details about pregnant journalist Charlotte Bellis's emergency MIQ application; she said she had not consented and disputed his account. In June 2022 he formally apologised for releasing personal information without consent and for inaccurate comments ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/covid-19-omicron-chris-hipkins-formally-apologises-over-charlotte-bellis-emergency-miq-saga/DX35AVZARU5RPUFTFUKDCNMK5A/)). - **Remarks about Bill English (2022):** apologised to former PM Bill English after suggesting in the House that English had favoured his brothers with government contracts ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/129959240/chris-hipkins-apologises-to-bill-english-for-dragging-family-into-debate)). - **As PM he dealt with several ministerial resignations/dismissals** — Stuart Nash, Meka Whaitiri, Michael Wood, Kiri Allan and Jan Tinetti's referral to the Privileges Committee (see those profiles). - **COVID vaccine advice for under-18s (2026):** the NZ Herald reported he had been briefed in March 2022 on advice to reduce the second-dose mandate for 12–17-year-olds; he initially denied receiving the Cabinet paper then said he had forgotten, and rejected Winston Peters' claim that he misled the COVID-19 Royal Commission ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/the-covid-vaccine-and-the-risk-to-under-18s-chris-hipkins-defends-not-making-advice-public/W3RWZP2RLVGLFJA3EUGNM62GDI/); [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/590823/labour-leader-chris-hipkins-denies-misleading-public-over-covid-vaccine-risk-to-under-18s)). ## 2026 candidacy - # Jacinda Ardern | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Former MP | | **Born** | 1980-07-26 — Hamilton, New Zealand | | **Electorate(s) held** | Mount Albert | | **Parliaments** | 49, 50, 51, 52, 53 | | **First elected** | 2008 | | **Key roles** | 40th Prime Minister of New Zealand (2017–2023)

17th Deputy Leader of the Labour Party (2017)
Member of the New Zealand Parliament (2008–2023) | | **Wikipedia** | [Jacinda Ardern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacinda_Ardern) | ## Current status Dame Jacinda Ardern left Parliament at the 2023 election and is not involved in the 2026 campaign as a candidate. After office she took up dual fellowships at the Harvard Kennedy School (2023) ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/new-zealand-jacinda-ardern-harvard-university-d9d82f742e79815e91687bd54213bd53)), became a trustee of Prince William's Earthshot Prize ([BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-65180096)), was appointed Special Envoy for the Christchurch Call by Chris Hipkins in April 2023 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/487340/former-pm-jacinda-ardern-appointed-as-christchurch-call-envoy)), and published her memoir *A Different Kind of Power* in June 2025, which won the 2026 E. H. McCormick Prize for best first book of general non-fiction ([NZ Book Awards](https://www.nzbookawards.nz/new-zealand-book-awards/2026-awards/winners/)). In February 2026 *The Guardian* reported that she and her family had moved to Sydney ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/feb/26/jacinda-ardern-living-in-australia-former-nz-new-zealand-pm)). She was made a Dame Grand Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit in 2023 ([DPMC](https://www.dpmc.govt.nz/publications/kings-birthday-and-coronation-honours-list-2023)). ## Biography Born 26 July 1980 in Hamilton and raised in Morrinsville and Murupara (her father was a police officer), Ardern joined Labour at 17 and graduated from the University of Waikato with a Bachelor of Communication Studies in 2001 ([Waikato University profile](https://apps.mngt.waikato.ac.nz/Newsroom/StudentProfile/3724)). She worked as a researcher for Phil Goff and Helen Clark, then in London as a policy adviser in the UK Cabinet Office, and in 2008 was elected president of the International Union of Socialist Youth. She was raised in the LDS Church but left it in 2005, citing her support for gay rights ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/lifestyle/news/article.cfm?c_id=6&objectid=11789352)). She married broadcaster Clarke Gayford in January 2024; their daughter Neve was born on 21 June 2018 while Ardern was prime minister ([BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-44568537)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2008–2011 | List | 20 | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | List | 13 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | List | 5 | Labour | | 51st | {{By-election link year|Mount Albert|2017}}– | Mount Albert | | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Mount Albert | 1 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Mount Albert | 1 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 40th Prime Minister of New Zealand | 26 October 2017 | 25 January 2023 | | | 17th Leader of the Labour Party | 1 August 2017 | 22 January 2023 | | | 36th Leader of the Opposition | 1 August 2017 | 26 October 2017 | | | 17th Deputy Leader of the Labour Party | 7 March 2017 | 1 August 2017 | | | Member of the New Zealand Parliament | 8 November 2008 | 15 April 2023 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ - **List MP, 2008–2017.** Entered Parliament from list position 20 in 2008 (losing the Waikato electorate). Stood in Auckland Central in 2011 and 2014, losing to National's Nikki Kaye by 717 and then 600 votes ([2011 results](http://www.electionresults.org.nz/electionresults_2011/electorate-1.html), [2014 results](http://www.electionresults.org.nz/electionresults_2014/electorate-1.html)). Spokesperson for youth affairs (under Goff), social development (No. 4 in Shearer's shadow cabinet, 2011), then justice, children, small business and arts (under Little, 2014). - **Mount Albert, 2017–2023.** Won the February 2017 Mount Albert by-election with about 77% of the vote ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=11807614)); majorities of 15,264 (2017) and 21,246 (2020) ([2017](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/electorate-details-27.html), [2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-24.html)). - **Deputy leader (7 Mar 2017) and leader (1 Aug 2017).** Became leader seven weeks before the 2017 election after Andrew Little resigned; Labour rose from 24% to the low 40s in polls ("Jacindamania") and won 46 seats ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=11922098)). - **Prime Minister, 26 Oct 2017 – 25 Jan 2023.** Led a Labour–NZ First coalition with Green confidence and supply (2017–2020), then the first single-party majority government under MMP after winning 65 seats and 50% of the party vote in 2020 ([Electoral Commission](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/)). Also Minister for National Security and Intelligence, Arts, Culture and Heritage, and the first Minister for Child Poverty Reduction. - **Resignation.** Announced on 19 January 2023 that she no longer had "enough in the tank", resigned as leader on 22 January and as PM on 25 January, and left Parliament in April 2023 ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/jan/19/jacinda-ardern-resigns-as-prime-minister-of-new-zealand)). ## Record & notable actions - **Christchurch mosque attacks (2019):** led the national response to the 15 March 2019 attacks in which 51 people were killed; within a month Parliament banned most semi-automatic weapons and high-capacity magazines, followed by a buy-back ([NYT](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/10/world/asia/new-zealand-guns-jacinda-ardern.html)); co-founded the Christchurch Call with Emmanuel Macron ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12226274)). - **COVID-19:** border closure (March 2020), alert-level 4 lockdown, elimination strategy until October 2021, vaccine rollout from February 2021 ([NYT](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/10/04/world/australia/new-zealand-covid-zero.html)). The MIQ system left many citizens unable to return; in April 2022 the High Court found aspects of MIQ unjustifiably limited citizens' right to enter New Zealand ([High Court judgment](https://www.courtsofnz.govt.nz/assets/Uploads/Judgments-online/2022-NZHC-832.pdf)). - **Child poverty and welfare:** Child Poverty Reduction Act targets; the 2018 Families Package (26 weeks' paid parental leave, Best Start payment) ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/feature/supporting-new-zealand-families-0)); free school lunches (Ka Ora, Ka Ako); benefit increases; first year of tertiary study fees-free (2018). - **Climate:** Zero Carbon Act passed with cross-party support (2019); declared a climate emergency in December 2020 ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/dec/02/new-zealand-declares-a-climate-change-emergency)). - **Tax:** ruled out a capital gains tax under her leadership in April 2019 after the Tax Working Group recommended one ([RNZ](https://www.radionz.co.nz/news/on-the-inside/387347/week-in-politics-labour-s-biggest-campaign-burden-scrapped)); bright-line test extended to 10 years (2021). - **Other:** formal apology for the Dawn Raids (2021); cannabis referendum (2020, narrowly defeated; she disclosed afterwards she voted yes) ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/123261775/pm-defends-no-comment-stance-on-cannabis-referendum)). - **Conscience votes:** voted for marriage equality (2013) and for the Abortion Legislation Act 2020 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/412087/abortion-legislation-bill-passes-third-and-final-reading-in-parliament)). ## Controversies - **Clare Curran (2018):** criticised for initially only removing Curran from Cabinet over an undisclosed meeting rather than dismissing her; Curran later resigned ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2018/09/prime-minister-jacinda-ardern-accepts-clare-curran-s-resignation-as-a-minister.html)). - **Labour staffer sexual-assault complaint (2019):** her account that she had been told the complaint did not involve sexual assault was questioned by media; party president Nigel Haworth resigned ([The Spinoff timeline](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/11-09-2019/timeline-labour-staffer-misconduct-inquiry/)). - **Hot-mic remark (2022):** called ACT leader David Seymour an "arrogant prick" in the House; she apologised and the pair later auctioned a framed copy for charity ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/130764372/jacinda-ardern-apologises-for-calling-david-seymour-an-arrogant-prick)). - **Undelivered targets:** critics, including former coalition partner Winston Peters, said her government under-delivered on housing (e.g. KiwiBuild), child poverty and inequality; her approval fell to 29% by late 2022 ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/dec/24/jacinda-arderns-popularity-plummeted-this-year-things-could-get-worse-in-2023); [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/new-zealands-ardern-leaves-legacy-kindness-disappointments-2023-01-19/)). - **Threats and abuse:** she was the target of sustained abuse and threats from anti-mandate protesters; a man was convicted of threatening to kill her ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/nz-news/350300416/richard-sivell-run-almost-two-years-appears-court)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - 3rd Leader of Mana Motuhake (2001–2003) | | **Wikipedia** | [Willie Jackson (politician)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Jackson_%28politician%29) | ## Current status Jackson is No. 4 on Labour's 2026 list (list-only) ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)) and, since the 11 March 2026 reshuffle, Labour's spokesperson for Māori development, Māori–Crown relations and associate health (Māori) ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360949687/hipkins-reshuffles-labour-portfolios-henare-departs-and-plan-hatched-maori-seats-race)). He has again led Labour's campaign for the Māori electorates; Labour won only one of the seven in 2023, after which he said he had considered quitting ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/senior-mp-willie-jackson-to-leave-politics-following-hefty-defeat-at-the-polls-but-only-if-hes-not-wanted/MTUJK4PQDJBKFNX7PZNZOCAPLY/)). ## Biography Born in 1961 (Ngāti Maniapoto, Ngāti Porou), the son of urban Māori leaders Dame June Jackson and Bob Jackson; his uncles included activist Syd Jackson and lawyer Moana Jackson ([The Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/atea/28-02-2019/the-incredible-legacy-of-dame-june-jackson)). After leaving Māngere College he became a freezing worker and, at 21, president of the freezing workers' union. In the 1990s he ran Tangata Records and managed Moana and the Moahunters. A broadcaster for two decades, he ran Radio Waatea and Urban Māori Broadcasting, hosted *Eye to Eye* (TV One, 2004–2009) and talkback on RadioLive with John Tamihere. He chaired the National Urban Māori Authority (from 2003) and led the Manukau Urban Māori Authority (from 2009), whose subsidiary won a charter-school contract in 2017 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/labour-candidate-willie-jackson-benefits-from-new-round-of-charter-schools/G676BTHOOKBLSAFRVUKYOFEZKE/)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 52nd | 2017–2020 | List | 22 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | List | 19 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–present | List | 9 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 27th Minister of Broadcasting and Media | 14 June 2022 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 45th Minister for Māori Development | 6 November 2020 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 17th Minister of Employment | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | 3rd Leader of Mana Motuhake | 2 June 2001 | 4 December 2003 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Opposition portfolios (as of 11 March 2026) Rank 5 in Chris Hipkins' shadow cabinet: - Spokesperson for Māori Development - Spokesperson for Māori Crown Relations - Associate Spokesperson for Health (Māori) _Source: [Shadow Cabinet of Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Chris_Hipkins), list as of 11 March 2026._ - **Alliance MP, 1999–2002** (Mana Motuhake); led Mana Motuhake from 2001 and was Alliance deputy leader at the 2002 election, when the party lost all its seats. - **Labour list MP, 2017–present.** Recruited by Andrew Little to run Labour's Māori-seat campaign in 2017, when Labour won all seven Māori electorates ([RNZ](http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/323829/willie-jackson-to-stand-for-labour)). - **Minister:** Minister of Employment (outside Cabinet) and Associate Minister for Māori Development, 2017–2020; Minister for Māori Development in Cabinet from November 2020, plus associate ACC and justice; Minister of Broadcasting and Media from June 2022 ([DPMC 2020](https://dpmc.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2020-11/ministerial-list-2-nov-2020.pdf)); co-chair of Labour's Māori caucus. - **Opposition:** Māori development, broadcasting, employment and associate portfolios (2023); Māori development and social development (March 2025); Māori development, Māori–Crown relations and associate health (Māori) (March 2026). ## Record & notable actions - **Public media merger:** introduced the Aotearoa New Zealand Public Media Bill to merge RNZ and TVNZ (2022); it was scrapped by the Hipkins government in February 2023 ([Parliament](https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/BILL_125298/aotearoa-new-zealand-public-media-bill); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/131174007/rnztvnz-merger-gone-minimum-wage-rises-policies-delayed-in-government-refocus)). - Apologised to Moriori on behalf of Ngāti Tama and Ngāti Mutunga as the Moriori Claims Settlement passed in 2021 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/moriori-praised-for-dedication-patience-as-18m-and-apology-settlement-with-crown-becomes-law/VR32NHE6MDBEHZE6ZL5Z2X5NDU/)). - A leading opponent of ACT's Treaty Principles Bill; won a 2024 Oxford Union debate calling for the return of mokomōkai from the British Museum ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2024/05/24/willie-jackson-calls-for-return-of-mokomokai-in-oxford-debate-win/)). ## Controversies - **Roast Busters interview (2013):** he and John Tamihere were taken off air at RadioLive after an interview with a friend of an alleged victim in which the group's actions were described as "mischief" ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/roast-busters-radiolive-hosts-taken-off-air/C4HJSTJI55U546Q2OUS4OA7WUY/?c_id=1&objectid=11155132)). - **Jack Tame interview (Dec 2022):** a combative Q+A interview on the media merger, in which he questioned the host's motives, drew criticism including from Ardern; he gave a partial apology ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/480223/willie-jackson-gives-partial-apology-over-public-media-merger-interview)). - **"Go to war" remark (Nov 2023):** said Māori would "go to war" if the incoming government pursued a Treaty principles referendum; ACT leader David Seymour responded that people who "threaten war" instead of debate "are not being a good actor" ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2023/11/labour-mp-willie-jackson-warns-of-m-ori-uprising-over-act-s-proposed-treaty-referendum.html)). - **Ejections from the House:** in December 2021 (refusing to withdraw calling ACT "right-wing fascists"), November 2024 (calling David Seymour a liar during the Treaty Principles Bill first reading) and May 2025 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/maori-development-minister-willie-jackson-kicked-out-of-parliament-for-right-wing-fascist-comment/OIZQJ3QM42VSM3GSSLE7YLLIYY/); [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/533792/watch-labour-s-willie-jackson-ejected-from-house-for-calling-david-seymour-a-liar-during-treaty-principles-bill-reading); [1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/05/15/labours-willie-jackson-booted-from-house/)). ## 2026 candidacy -
